lesson_title: One Company, Four Statements, Every Mark
hook_text: A bakery slice the books value at 392 cents sells between cousins for 460. Who is wrong?
clip_script: A family bakery became a company — six hundred thousand slices of ownership. The books are honest: everything the bakery owns, minus everything it owes, comes to 392 cents a slice. Yet cousins pay 460 cents. Sixty-eight cents above the honest number. Are they fools? No — they are buying what the books are forbidden to record: the corner location, the customers who queue every morning, next year's loaves. The books look backward; the price looks forward. Now flip the question the examiner loves. Each slice EARNED 73 cents this year — that is earnings per share. Each slice was PAID 54 cents — that is the dividend. The missing 19 cents did not vanish; it stayed inside, making every slice quietly heavier. And the family money itself? It earned 21,2 cents per rand while a bank deposit pays about eight — thirteen cents of reward for risk. Meanwhile the bakery borrows at ten and puts the money to work earning 25,3. Every borrowed rand earns more than it eats. That is the whole of Paper 1 analysis: two numbers, same units, one comparison, one judgement. Books against market. Earned against paid. Business against bank. Loan cost against return. Master those four comparisons and the analysis question becomes the friendliest marks on the paper.
visual_style: A bread slice split into layered coins — book value stacking to 392, a golden 68-cent halo appearing above it; then a balance beam weighing 73 earned against 54 paid, with 19 cents sliding back into the loaf.
pacing: Curious open on the price gap, steady reveal of the halo, brisk drumbeat through the four comparisons.
call_to_action: Watch the full revision session and walk into Paper 1 with all four comparisons in your pocket.
